For each named finite classical model in this page, adopt the preparation explicitly stated in its theorem. In a canonical branch, take a measurable phase space with a specified reference measure $
u$, a measurable Hamiltonian $H$, an inverse energy parameter $ eta>0$, and a finite positive partition function $Z=\int e^{- eta H}\,d
u$; the adopted probability measure is $dP=Z^{-1}e^{- eta H}\,d
u$. In a grand-canonical branch, take disjoint particle-number sectors with sector partition functions $Z_N$ and a dimensionless activity $z>0$ for which $\Xi=\sum_{N\ge0}z^N Z_N$ is finite; sector $N$ has probability weight $z^N Z_N/\Xi$. The spherical-shell and product preparations are separate explicitly specified probability laws in their consuming theorem statements. These are alternative model assumptions, not consequences of a Hamiltonian flow and not assertions that a laboratory system realizes them.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

A **real random variable** on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is a function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. Its range $X(\Omega)$ is finite. The **distribution** or **law** of $X$ is the finite probability space on $X(\Omega)$ with
$$\mathbb P_X(x):=\mathbb P(\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)=x\}).$$
The weights $\mathbb P_X(x)$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$ because the fibres of $X$ form a finite partition of $\Omega$ ([[thm-finite-additivity-of-probability]]).

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

For a finite real random variable $X$, its **moment generating function** is the everywhere-defined function
$$M_X(t):=\mathbb E[\exp(tX)],\qquad t\in\mathbb R.$$
Finiteness of the outcome space makes this a finite sum, so no convergence hypothesis is needed.
This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

For every $\alpha>0$,
$$\lim_{x\to+\infty}\frac{\log x}{x^\alpha}=0.$$

Let $(\Omega,w)$ be a finite probability space: $\Omega$ is a finite set, each weight $w(\omega)$ is nonnegative, and $\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1$. Let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a real random variable and let $\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega)$. Its **variance** is

$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}(X(\omega)-\mathbb E[X])^2w(\omega).$$

All sums are finite, so the definition requires no additional integrability or moment hypothesis.

derivations.claim: The total weight is $\prod_{i=1}^n(p+(1-p))=1$, so the stipulated weights form a finite probability law. Summing over all coordinates except $i$ gives $P(X_i=1)=p$ and $P(X_i=0)=1-p$; the product factorization also gives independence. For $0\le k\le n$ put $c_{n,k}:=\#\{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}:|S|=k\}$. The set of coordinates with value $1$ gives a bijection between outcomes with $K=k$ and such subsets, so $P(K=k)=c_{n,k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. By [F4] and [F12], $\mathbb E X_i=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\mathbb E[(X_i-p)^2]=p(1-p)$. For $i\ne j$, the product weights factor the finite sum, giving $\mathbb E[(X_i-p)(X_j-p)]=\mathbb E(X_i-p)\mathbb E(X_j-p)=0$. Expanding $K$ and $(K-np)^2$ therefore yields $\mathbb E K=np$ and $\operatorname{Var}(K)=np(1-p)$.

The finite-sum definition [F5] and product weights give $$M_K(s)=\sum_{x\in\Omega_n}P_p(x)e^{s\sum_i x_i}=\prod_{i=1}^n\bigl((1-p)+pe^s\bigr)=(1-p+pe^s)^n.$$ This is a finite factorization, so no limiting interchange is involved.

On $0<a<1$, differentiating the displayed expression for $D$ with [F9] gives $D(p\Vert p)=0$, $\partial_aD(a\Vert p)|_{a=p}=0$, and $\partial_a^2D(a\Vert p)=1/[a(1-a)]\ge4$, since $a(1-a)\le1/4$. Let $G(a)=D(a\Vert p)-2(a-p)^2$. Then $G(p)=G'(p)=0$ and $G''\ge0$. For $a>p$, the mean value theorem applied first to $G'$ and then to $G$ gives $G'(a)\ge0$ and $G(a)\ge0$; for $a<p$, the same two applications give $G'(a)\le0$ and again $G(a)\ge0$. Thus $D(a\Vert p)\ge2(a-p)^2$ for interior $a$. At $a\downarrow0$, the only noncontinuous-looking term is $a\log a=-\log(1/a)/(1/a)$, which tends to zero by [F11]; at $a\uparrow1$ the analogous term is $(1-a)\log(1-a)$. The remaining factors are continuous, so the endpoint extensions preserve the inequality.

Fix $1\le k\le n-1$ and let $a=k/n$. For $0\le j\le n$ put $q_j=c_{n,j}a^j(1-a)^{n-j}$. These are the count probabilities under the finite product weights with parameter $a$; their sum is $1$ by factoring the total weight as $(a+(1-a))^n$. For each $0\le j<n$, count pairs $(S,T)$ with $S\subset T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $|S|=j$, and $|T|=j+1$. Choosing $S$ first gives $c_{n,j}(n-j)$ pairs, while choosing $T$ first gives $c_{n,j+1}(j+1)$; hence $c_{n,j+1}/c_{n,j}=(n-j)/(j+1)$. Therefore $$\frac{q_{j+1}}{q_j}=\frac{n-j}{j+1}\frac{a}{1-a}.$$ The factor $(n-j)/(j+1)$ decreases strictly with $j$, since $(n-j-1)(j+1)<(n-j)(j+2)$ for $j<n-1$. At $j=k-1$ the ratio is $(n-k+1)/(n-k)>1$, and at $j=k$ it is $k/(k+1)<1$. Thus the sequence increases through $q_k$ and decreases after it, so $q_k$ is the largest of its $n+1$ masses. Their sum is $1$, whence $1/(n+1)\le q_k\le1$.

Pointwise on $\Omega_n$, $\mathbf 1_{\{|\overline X-p|\ge\varepsilon\}}\le (\overline X-p)^2/\varepsilon^2$. Summing this inequality with the finite weights and using step 1.1 gives the first probability bound.

Suppose first $p<a<1$ and put $s=\log\!\bigl(a(1-p)/(p(1-a))\bigr)>0$. On $\{K\ge na\}$, $e^{sK}\ge e^{sna}$, so the finite expectation of the nonnegative random variable $e^{sK}$ is at least $e^{sna}P_p(K\ge na)$. By step 1.2, $$P_p(K\ge na)\le e^{-sna}(1-p+pe^s)^n=e^{-nD(a\Vert p)},$$ where $e^s=a(1-p)/(p(1-a))$, $1-p+pe^s=(1-p)/(1-a)$, and [F7]–[F8] simplify the logarithm. If $0<a<p$, the same value of $s$ is negative; on $\{K\le na\}$ one again has $e^{sK}\ge e^{sna}$, and the same substitution yields $P_p(K\le na)\le e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}$. This proves both exponential tail bounds without using a general concentration theorem as a premise.

Direct division of the two point probabilities, using the same subset count $c_{n,k}$ from step 1.1, gives $$\frac{P_p(K=k)}{q_k}=\left(\frac pa\right)^k\left(\frac{1-p}{1-a}\right)^{n-k}.$$ Since $k=na$ and $n-k=n(1-a)$, [F7]–[F8] give the logarithm of this ratio as $n a\log(p/a)+n(1-a)\log((1-p)/(1-a))=-nD(a\Vert p)$, so the ratio is $e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}$. Combining with step 2.1 proves the claimed bounds for $1\le k\le n-1$. For $k=0$ and $k=n$, direct evaluation gives $P_p(K=0)=(1-p)^n=e^{-nD(0\Vert p)}$ and $P_p(K=n)=p^n=e^{-nD(1\Vert p)}$, which satisfy the same inequalities.

If $0<\varepsilon<1$, split the deviation event into the upper threshold $a_+=p+\varepsilon$ and lower threshold $a_-=p-\varepsilon$. For an interior threshold apply step 2.3 and then step 1.3; at $a_+=1$ or $a_-=0$ use the exact endpoint probability $p^n$ or $(1-p)^n$ and the endpoint case of step 1.3; a threshold outside $[0,1]$ gives an empty event. Each nonempty tail is at most $e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$, so their sum is at most $2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$. If $\varepsilon\ge1$, the deviation event is empty because $0\le\overline X\le1$ and $0<p<1$.

If $k_n/n\to a\in(0,1)$, then $D(k_n/n\Vert p)\to D(a\Vert p)$ by continuity on $(0,1)$. Taking logarithms of step 3.1 and dividing by $n$ bounds $n^{-1}\log P_p(K=k_n)$ between $-D(k_n/n\Vert p)-\log(n+1)/n$ and $-D(k_n/n\Vert p)$. By [F11], $\log(n+1)/n\to0$, so the squeeze theorem gives the stated rate. These probabilities remain conditional on the explicitly stipulated product law; no finite sample or measurement is asserted.

derivations.claim: If this family were product-additive under the definition in the Statement, its fixed alphabet would have $|\Gamma|=|\Omega_1|=6$, forcing $|\Omega_2|=|\Gamma|^2=36$. But $|\Omega_2|=1+1+4^2=18$. Thus no such product decomposition exists. The three sector weights in the finite exponential tilt are $1$, $x$, and $4^Nx^2$, where $x=e^{-\beta N\epsilon}>0$; they sum to the displayed positive finite $Z_N(\beta)$, so division by $Z_N$ gives a finite probability law as in [F10]. For $\beta>0$, [A1] and [F1] identify this normalized counting weight with the adopted canonical branch; for $\beta\le0$ it remains only the stated algebraic expression.

The energies of $A_N$ and $C_N$ differ from $N\epsilon$ by exactly $N\epsilon$. The condition $\Delta<N\epsilon$ excludes both sectors from $\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}$, while $B_N\subseteq\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}$. Thus the shell is exactly the one-state set $B_N$ and its uniform counting probability assigns $B_N$ probability one.

Put $M_N=\max\{1,4^Nx^2\}$. If $x\le1$, then $x\le M_N$; if $x>1$, then $4^Nx^2\ge x$ since $N\ge1$. Hence $M_N\le Z_N\le3M_N$. By [F2]–[F3], $$\frac1N\log M_N=\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\}=\psi(\beta),$$ so taking logarithms in $M_N\le Z_N\le3M_N$ gives $0\le\psi_N-\psi\le(\log3)/N$, and consequently $\psi_N\to\psi$.

By [F4], $\exp$ is a power series converging for every real argument, so [F6] makes $\exp$ real analytic on $\mathbb R$. The affine polynomial $\beta\mapsto-\beta N\epsilon$ is real analytic, hence [F7] makes $\beta\mapsto e^{-\beta N\epsilon}$ real analytic as well.
Since $(1-2^Nx)^2\ge0$, $1+4^Nx^2\ge2^{N+1}x$. Therefore $Z_N=1+x+4^Nx^2\ge(2^{N+1}+1)x$, and division by $Z_N>0$ gives $P_{\beta,N}(B_N)\le(2^{N+1}+1)^{-1}$.

The equality $\log4=2\log2$ from [F3] gives the unique corner $\beta_c=(\log2)/\epsilon>0$. On $0<\beta<\beta_c$, the larger branch is $\log4-2\beta\epsilon$ and has slope $-2\epsilon$; on $\beta>\beta_c$ the larger branch is $0$ and has slope $0$. The one-sided slopes differ.

The exponential is positive, so $Z_N=1+e^{-\beta N\epsilon}+4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon}>0$ for every real $\beta$. Its expression as a sum and product of the analytic function in step 1.4 is real analytic by [F7].

By [F12], with [F11] identifying $H_N$ as a finite real random variable, the mean energy per member is $u_N(\beta)=\epsilon\bigl(x+2\cdot4^Nx^2\bigr)/Z_N$ for $\beta>0$. If $0<\beta<\beta_c$, divide numerator and denominator by the high-sector weight $4^Nx^2$: the low-to-high ratio is $e^{-N(\log4-2\beta\epsilon)}\to0$ and the middle-to-high ratio is $e^{N(\beta\epsilon-\log4)}\le2^{-N}\to0$, so $u_N(\beta)\to2\epsilon$. If $\beta>\beta_c$, both non-low weights $x=e^{-\beta N\epsilon}$ and $4^Nx^2=e^{N(\log4-2\beta\epsilon)}$ tend to zero, so $u_N(\beta)\to0$. At $\beta=\beta_c$, the three sector weights are $1$, $2^{-N}$, and $1$, so $u_N(\beta_c)=\epsilon(2^{-N}+2)/(2+2^{-N})\to\epsilon$. These limits give the stated piecewise $u$ and its unequal one-sided limits.

Fix $\beta_0\in\mathbb R$ and put $z_0=Z_N(\beta_0)>0$. By step 1.4, $\exp$ is real analytic; [F9] gives $\exp'(\log z_0)=z_0\ne0$, so [F8] gives a real-analytic local inverse near $z_0$. By the inverse definition [F2], that local inverse is $\log$ on this neighborhood, hence $\log$ is real analytic near $z_0$.

By [F5] the target property is real analyticity, and [F7] makes the composition $N^{-1}\log Z_N$ real analytic using steps 2.3 and 3.2. Hence every finite-$N$ function $\psi_N$ is real analytic. The derivative jump in step 2.2 belongs to the limiting function, not to a finite-$N$ singularity.

separate continuity condition at $a$: for every $\varepsilon>0$, all
domain points $x$ sufficiently near $a$ satisfy
$|f(x)-f(a)|<\varepsilon$.

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology
([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]]); we write
$[t]:=q(t)=t+\mathbb Z$. Thus $[s]=[t]$ exactly when $s-t\in\mathbb Z$. The map
$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if
$s,t\in[0,1)$ satisfy $s-t\in\mathbb Z$, then $|s-t|<1$ forces $s=t$.
Consequently the map $[0,1)\to\mathbb T$, $t\mapsto[t]$, is a bijection.

**Topological checks.** The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and maps onto $\mathbb T$, so the quotient is compact by [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is continuous by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], and is constant on quotient fibres by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]. It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. In particular $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff.

The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. The images under $q$ of rational-endpoint open intervals form a countable base: if $q(t)\in V$ with $V$ open, choose such an interval containing $t$ and contained in $q^{-1}[V]$. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

**The measure.** For a Borel set $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of
$\mathbb R$, because $q$ is continuous
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue
measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Define

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

the value at $q^{-1}[E]$ of the same-ambient restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $[0,1)$
([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

This is a measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$ by [[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]:
the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). The assignment agrees with
$E\mapsto m_{\mathbb T}(E)$ on indicators, and it is additive and homogeneous on
finite nonnegative simple functions; for a sequence $0\le F_0\le F_1\le\cdots$
with $F_n\uparrow F$ pointwise the identity passes to the limit because
$F_n\circ q\uparrow F\circ q$ and monotone convergence holds for $\lambda_1$
([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable
$F$ the integral is defined by decomposition into nonnegative parts or into real
and imaginary parts, and it is linear
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). In particular
$\int_{\mathbb T}1\,dm_{\mathbb T}=1$, and the same formula holds with $[0,1)$
replaced by any half-open interval $[a,a+1)$ or $(a,a+1]$, by the periodicity of
$q^{-1}[E]$ and the translation invariance of $\lambda_1$
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Translation invariance.** For $y\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\tau_y:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$, $\tau_y([t]):=[t+y]$, is well defined (if
$s-t\in\mathbb Z$ then $(s+y)-(t+y)\in\mathbb Z$) and continuous, because it is
induced by the continuous map $t\mapsto q(t+y)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb T$. This composite is constant on the fibres of $q$, since $q(t)=q(s)$ implies $q(t+y)=q(s+y)$ ([[thm-quotient-universal-property]]). It preserves
$m_{\mathbb T}$: write $y=n+r$ with $n=\lfloor y\rfloor$ and $r\in[0,1)$, put
$A:=q^{-1}[E]$ and use that $A-n=A$ and that
$A\cap[0,1)=\bigl(A\cap[0,r)\bigr)\cup\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)$ while
$A\cap[r,r+1)=\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)\cup\bigl((A\cap[0,r))+1\bigr)$, so that

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

the middle equality by translation invariance of $\lambda_1$. Hence
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving
system for every $y$, and the published integral-invariance theorem gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put
$\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ with the quotient topology of the
canonical projection $q_n$, and define

$$m_{\mathbb T^n}(E):=\lambda_n\bigl(q_n^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)^n\bigr),\qquad \int_{\mathbb T^n}F\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}:=\int_{[0,1)^n}F\circ q_n\,d\lambda_n .$$

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

Let $\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\Lambda$ be a flat translation torus, where $\Lambda$ is a full-rank lattice, and let $\mu=c\,da$ be its fixed translation-invariant volume measure in dimensionless translation coordinates, with $c>0$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$. Suppose $\chi_t:\mathbb T^n\to\mathbb T^n$ is a jointly $C^2$ family of diffeomorphisms with $\chi_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $C^1$ velocity field $b$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}b=0$ in local translation charts. Let $f_0\in C^1(\mathbb T^n)$ satisfy $0<m\le f_0\le M<\infty$ and $\int f_0\,d\mu=1$, and define $f_t:=f_0\circ\chi_t^{-1}$. Then $f_t$ is a probability density for every $t\in I$, the integral $H(f_t):=-\int_{\mathbb T^n}f_t\log f_t\,d\mu$ is finite, and $H(f_t)=H(f_0)$. Here $H$ is the dimensionless fine entropy of this density; multiplication by a physical constant such as $k_B$ is a separate interpretation.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $(\Omega,w)$ be a finite probability space: $\Omega$ is a finite set, each weight $w(\omega)$ is nonnegative, and $\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1$. Let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a real random variable and let $\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega)$. Its **variance** is

$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}(X(\omega)-\mathbb E[X])^2w(\omega).$$

All sums are finite, so the definition requires no additional integrability or moment hypothesis.

derivations.claim: Under the product-preparation convention [F1], for a fixed $j$ the uniform weight on $\{-1,1\}^{n_j}$ is a probability law, including the singleton case $n_j=0$. Each increment has mean zero and square one by [F2]–[F4]. Independence follows from the product weights, so the cross terms in $\mathbb E(\sum_i\Xi_i)^2$ vanish; hence $\mathbb E S_j=0$ and, by [F19], $\operatorname{Var}(S_j)=n_j\ell_j^2$. Conditioning on the last increment gives $u_{n+1}(r)=\tfrac12u_n(r-1)+\tfrac12u_n(r+1)$, with the stated initial mass.

For the rotor, write $R_s(q)=q+p_0s/I$ modulo $2\pi$. At $T=2\pi I/|p_0|$, the angle increment is $2\pi$ when $p_0>0$ and $-2\pi$ when $p_0<0$, so $R_T$ is the identity. The stated full AC includes the countable-choice assumption of [F16]. For every Borel $E\subseteq\mathcal X$, $\iota_{p_0}^{-1}(\Phi_s^{-1}E)=R_s^{-1}(\iota_{p_0}^{-1}E)$; translation invariance in [F16] therefore gives $\mu_0(\Phi_s^{-1}E)=\mu_0(E)$, and in particular $\mu_0$ is invariant under the rotor flow.

Under the four-state pushforward, the first three probability vectors are $$\pi_0=(1/2,1/2,0,0),\quad \pi_1=(0,1/2,1/2,0),\quad \pi_2=(0,0,1/2,1/2).$$ The map $\mathcal T$ is a permutation, so it maps the uniform reference weights $1/4$ to themselves; it also leaves the multiset of the evolving fine probabilities unchanged, and each fine entropy is $-\tfrac12\log\tfrac12-\tfrac12\log\tfrac12=\log2$. The coarse cell probabilities for $\{\{0,1\},\{2,3\}\}$ are $(1,0)$, $(1/2,1/2)$, and $(0,1)$, giving coarse entropies $0,\log2,0$ under the zero-term convention. This proves the stated decrease.

By independence and [F5], the characteristic function is $$\varphi_{S_j}(k)=\prod_{i=1}^{n_j}\mathbb E(e^{ik\ell_j\Xi_i})=\cos(\ell_j k)^{n_j}.$$ Fix $k$. Continuity of cosine and $\cos0=1$ make $\cos u>0$ for all sufficiently small $|u|$. For such $u$, put $f(u)=\log\cos u$. By the chain rule, $f'(u)=-\sin u/\cos u$ and $f'(0)=0$. From [F10], $\sin u/u\to\sin'(0)=1$ and $\cos u\to1$, so the difference quotient $f'(u)/u=-\sin u/(u\cos u)$ tends to $-1$; hence $f''(0)=-1$. The same derivative rules make $f$ twice differentiable on a neighbourhood of zero, so [F15] gives $\log\cos u=-u^2/2+o(u^2)$. For $t>0$, $n_j\delta t_j\to t$ because $0\le t-n_j\delta t_j<\delta t_j$, and therefore $$n_j\log\cos(\ell_jk)=-\frac{n_j\ell_j^2k^2}{2}+n_j\,o(\ell_j^2)\longrightarrow-Dtk^2.$$ Indeed $n_j\ell_j^2=2D n_j\delta t_j\to2Dt$, so $n_j\ell_j^2$ is bounded, while $o(\ell_j^2)/\ell_j^2\to0$; their product proves the remainder tends to zero. For $t=0$, $n_j=0$ and every law is $\delta_0$. Thus in all cases $\varphi_{S_j}(k)\to e^{-Dtk^2}=\varphi_{N(0,2Dt)}(k)$ for every real $k$, using [F6]–[F7] for the target law.

The measure definition gives $\mu_0(A)=\nu([0,\pi))=1/2$. At each $s=mT$, $\Phi_s$ is the identity on the support of $\mu_0$, so $\mu_0(A\cap\Phi_s^{-1}A)=1/2\ne1/4=\mu_0(A)^2$, contradicting the mixing condition stated in the Statement. For $q_0=[\theta_0]$, the function $g([\theta],p)=\cos(\theta-\theta_0)$ is well-defined and continuous on the quotient because cosine is continuous and $2\pi$-periodic, and it is bounded by $1$. Its values are $1$ at times $mT$ and $-1$ at times $mT+T/2$, so its expectation has no limit. By [F18], weak convergence would force convergence of this expectation, so the evolving point laws have no weak limit.

The mathematical result [F17] assumes a smooth diffeomorphic flow on a flat torus, divergence-free velocity, and a positive bounded $C^1$ density. The atomic four-state law in step 1.3 is not such a density or flow; its coarse-entropy decrease neither invokes nor contradicts that fine differential-entropy result. It establishes no monotonicity law for other coarse-graining procedures.

The right-hand side of step 2.1 is the characteristic function of the specified Borel probability $N(0,2Dt)$. Apply the reverse implication of [F8] to the Borel laws of $S_j$ to obtain weak convergence. The only non-finite-choice strength used here is the full AC explicitly carried by [F7]–[F9]; the finite product construction is in step 1.1 and its pointwise characteristic calculation is in step 2.1.

The walk limit in steps 1.1–2.1 concerns only fixed-time marginal laws under the stated independent-increment scaling; no path-space limit, deterministic collision limit, experiment, observed frequency, or empirical inference is part of the hypotheses or conclusion.

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $p\in(0,1)$, and give $\Omega_n=\{0,1\}^n$ the explicitly stipulated product probability whose singleton weights are
$$P_p(\{(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\})=\prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i};$$
for an event $A\subseteq\Omega_n$, $P_p(A)$ is the sum of these weights over $x\in A$.
Write $X_i(x)=x_i$, $K=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$, and $\overline X=K/n$. These variables and all probabilities are dimensionless. The product law is an adopted sampling model; independence is an assumption of that law, not an inference about any apparatus or equilibrium system.

For $a\in(0,1)$ define the Bernoulli relative-entropy rate
$$D(a\Vert p)=a\log\frac ap+(1-a)\log\frac{1-a}{1-p},$$
and set $D(0\Vert p)=-\log(1-p)$ and $D(1\Vert p)=-\log p$. Then
$$\mathbb E K=np,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=np(1-p),$$
and for every dimensionless $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_p\bigl(|\overline X-p|\ge\varepsilon\bigr)\le\frac{p(1-p)}{n\varepsilon^2},\qquad P_p\bigl(|\overline X-p|\ge\varepsilon\bigr)\le 2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}.$$
For $p<a<1$ and $0<a<p$, respectively,
$$P_p(K\ge na)\le e^{-nD(a\Vert p)},\qquad P_p(K\le na)\le e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}.$$
For each integer $0\le k\le n$, putting $a=k/n$ gives the point-mass bounds
$$\frac1{n+1}e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}\le P_p(K=k)\le e^{-nD(a\Vert p)}.$$
Consequently, for every sequence of integers $k_n\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ with $k_n/n\to a\in(0,1)$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log P_p(K=k_n)=-D(a\Vert p).$$
All conclusions are conditional calculations for this finite product model and make no claim that physical outcomes are independent or that a small model probability is a logical contradiction.

For $\varepsilon=1/10$, the Chebyshev bound is $(3/16)/(100/100)=3/16$, while the exponential bound is $2e^{-2}$. These are upper bounds on a specified model probability, not results from 100 recorded trials.

For $k=35$, $a=k/n=7/20$ and $$D(7/20\Vert1/4)=\frac7{20}\log\frac75+\frac{13}{20}\log\frac{13}{15}.$$ The point-mass estimate in [F1] therefore reads $$\frac1{101}e^{-100D(7/20\Vert1/4)}\le P_{1/4}(K=35)\le e^{-100D(7/20\Vert1/4)}.$$ This finite example displays the polynomial prefactor and common exponential rate without numerical fitting or empirical inference.

Use counting measure on each $\Omega_N$ as the reference measure, so every individual state has weight one. For a real inverse-energy parameter $\beta$ in joules$^{-1}$, define the finite exponential-tilt probability by
$$Z_N(\beta)=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_N}e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}=1+e^{-\beta N\epsilon}+4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon},\qquad P_{\beta,N}(\omega)=\frac{e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}}{Z_N(\beta)}.$$
For $\beta>0$ this is the adopted canonical preparation. For $\beta\le0$ it is only the same finite counting formula used algebraically; no negative-temperature reservoir is asserted. Also, for a shell half-width $\Delta$ in joules with $0\le\Delta<N\epsilon$, define $\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}=\{\omega:|H_N(\omega)-N\epsilon|\le\Delta\}$ and give it the uniform counting probability $Q_{N,\Delta}(\omega)=|\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}|^{-1}$ for $\omega\in\mathcal S_{N,\Delta}$.

The shell centered at $4\epsilon$ with half-width $\Delta<4\epsilon$ excludes the neighboring energy levels $0$ and $8\epsilon$, so it contains exactly the single state in $B_4$. Its uniform probability is therefore one on $B_4$, compared with the canonical value $1/33$.

citations.quote: **Finite coarse-entropy model.** Let $\Omega=\{0,1,2,3\}$ with uniform reference probability and permutation $\mathcal T(0)=1,\mathcal T(1)=2,\mathcal T(2)=3,\mathcal T(3)=0$. Start from $\pi_0=(1/2,1/2,0,0)$, and evolve by pushforward under $\mathcal T$. For the coarse partition $\{\{0,1\},\{2,3\}\}$, let $(r_1,r_2)$ be any probability vector with $r_i\ge0$ and $r_1+r_2=1$, and define its coarse Shannon entropy by $H_c(r_1,r_2)=-\sum_{i:r_i>0}r_i\log r_i$ in nats. Define fine entropy analogously for a probability vector on the four states, using $0\log0=0$. The coarse entropies at times $0,1,2$ are $0,\log2,0$, while the fine entropy is $\log2$ at all three times.
